title: Quantum query–space tradeoffs for collisions and distinctness
formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the functions \(T_b(n,m,S)\) for \(b\in\{\mathrm{collision},\mathrm{distinctness}\}\): the minimum worst-case number of quantum queries needed by an algorithm with at most \(S\) qubits of total retained memory to solve the specified decision problem with error at most \(1/3\). The input is an oracle for \(f:[n]\to[m]\). In the collision problem, \(n\) is even and \(f\) is promised to be either injective or exactly two-to-one; distinguish these cases. In element distinctness there is no promise; decide whether \(f\) is injective. The full parameter domain is \(m\ge n\ge2\) and \(S\ge4(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil)+10\), with integer parameters. This card selects the source's total-memory tradeoff, allowing all retained memory to be quantum; separating classical and quantum memory budgets is a further variant.
why: Quantum collision and distinctness algorithms gain speed while retaining substantial information about queried values. Their optimal time/space tradeoffs would quantify how much memory is necessary for those advantages and develop lower-bound methods for problems whose output contains only one bit.
status_note: Open in the 2021 source. Checked on 2026-09-14: the February 2026 work concerns nested collision finding; the September 2026 preprint gives claimed search bounds under label symmetry and explicitly leaves removal of symmetry open. Neither checked statement settles the unrestricted, worst-case decision tradeoff formulated here. The total-memory convention is explicit.

progress.text: Aaronson lists the two query/space tradeoffs as open, distinguishing them from the already established unrestricted-query complexities.
Hao, Huang and Liu give space-sensitive lower bounds for nested collision finding, addressing a related short-output barrier.

Magniez and Zur post claimed tight search tradeoffs under label symmetry and explicitly retain the unrestricted-algorithm question. These are restricted-model progress, not a resolution of the displayed decision curves.

importance.reason: Characterizes simultaneous time and memory limits for basic quantum collision tasks, beyond query complexity alone.

sentences: The question asks for the optimal quantum query cost of collision testing and element distinctness at every allowed memory budget.
The oracle returns an output symbol, and the algorithm must decide the answer with bounded worst-case error.
All retained storage counts, including classical tables and query registers.
Recent lower bounds concern nested collision tasks or search algorithms restricted by label symmetry.
The target remains matching upper and lower bounds for unrestricted algorithms solving the two decision problems.

definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Injective means that distinct inputs have distinct outputs. Exactly two-to-one means that every value in the image has exactly two preimages; unused output values have none. The required output is one bit, not a pair of colliding indices.

Let \(a=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) and \(v=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil\). A query maps \(|i,y,z\rangle\) to \(|i,y\mathbin{\oplus}\operatorname{enc}(f(i)),z\rangle\), with \(a\) address qubits, \(v\) answer qubits and a remaining work register. Here \(\operatorname{enc}\) is the length-\(v\) binary encoding and \(\oplus\) is bitwise addition modulo two. For address zero or an address larger than \(n\), use the all-zero answer. One call returns one entire output symbol and costs one query. The address and answer registers are included in \(S\).

An algorithm begins with an input-independent state on at most \(S\) qubits, alternates a fixed finite sequence of input-independent quantum channels with oracle calls, and ends with a two-outcome measurement. A density matrix describes its state. An allowed intervening channel has the form \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\), where the finitely many matrices satisfy \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\); it maps the retained memory back into the same bounded space. This allows measurement, randomization and resetting memory. Discarded information cannot be retrieved later. Any measurement outcomes, classical work bits, or tables that remain accessible must occupy the counted memory. Input-dependent classical control is therefore also stored in that memory. There is no external input-dependent advice, second oracle, or uncounted read/write storage.

The channels and measurement may depend on \(b,n,m,S\), but not on \(f\). Their descriptions and the input-independent instruction index are not workspace, and no uniformity, gate-count or computation-time restriction is imposed between queries. Arbitrary computation on the stored memory, including coherent access to stored tables, is free. All oracle calls count, including preprocessing and calls on branches later discarded. The finite query budget is worst-case, and correctness must hold on every valid oracle, with probability at least \(2/3\). The stated space floor allows elementary repeated scans, so both minima are finite; no upper limit on \(S\) is imposed.
answer_criterion: Supply positive functions \(H_b(n,m,S)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(cH_b(n,m,S)\le T_b(n,m,S)\le CH_b(n,m,S)\) for both tasks throughout their parameter domains. Both algorithms and matching lower bounds must respect the stated memory budget; an unrecorded increase in space is not allowed. The functions must describe the asymptotic dependence on the parameters, not simply repeat the optimization defining \(T_b\). Bounds for collision search, random inputs, or label-symmetric algorithms alone do not establish the required worst-case decision tradeoffs.

context_blocks.text: Without a restrictive memory budget, the familiar quantum query scales are \(n^{1/3}\) for the collision promise and \(n^{2/3}\) for element distinctness in their standard parameter regimes. Their optimality as query bounds does not determine the memory needed to attain them.

A classical table that can be queried coherently still occupies memory in this formulation. Counting its bits prevents a large external table from making a small-qubit algorithm appear to use little total storage. The separate question of which part of the storage must preserve quantum coherence is not resolved by a total-space bound.

The February 2026 work establishes memory lower bounds for a nested collision task with short output. Its input uses an additional oracle and a different success condition, so its lower bounds are not automatically the tradeoffs for either decision problem defined here.

The September 2026 preprint claims tight bounds for collision search and element-distinctness search under a label-symmetry restriction. Its Section 1.4 explicitly leaves removal of that restriction open. Permuting labels to symmetrize an arbitrary algorithm may require additional memory, which prevents treating symmetry as free.
